> **Dinesh:** it's amazing there's no motion!

Why? Unless they were alive and moving on their own or one had air currents moving across the table and moving them during the exposure, there won't be any motion. If you have either of those cases, you've got other problems than using cloth in your holograms.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:d7565ec10c="MichaelH"][quote:d7565ec10c="Dinesh"]it's amazing there's no motion![/quote:d7565ec10c]

Why? Unless they were alive and moving on their own or one had air currents moving across the table and moving them during the exposure, there won't be any motion. If you have either of those cases, you've got other problems than using cloth in your holograms.[/quote:d7565ec10c]

Cloth has a constantly shifting weight and is not rigid at all. The very small shifts due to thermal currents (some arisingg from thas laser itself) and creasing effects cause motion in cloth. Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn't. If the sails were a stiff plastic it'll probably work. Since it does, I have to assume that either Andres had a pretty powerful laser or the sails were stiff or he was lucky. Please understand I'm not "putting down" his hologram. I think it's great! I'm glad that he's posted it!

Some materials do seem to move "on their own". This is why so many have tried making a hologram of a rose and going through all sorts of gyrations to stop it moving. Freezing it liquid nitrogen, spraying it with hair spray etc. Many years ago at Icon holographics there was a lady who owned a doll shop near the studios. It was decided to make a "doll's House" hologram of her dolls inside the house. Kaveh will know the details. Anyway, these dolls were dressed in very fine material - fine cotton or silk, I think. Anyway, it was very difficult not to get motion. I remember Tuffy, the holographer, shooed us all away from the lab and settled for hours. I also remember we were only too glad to be "shooed away" into the Icon pub across the road

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** Cloth has a constantly shifting weight...

That's too broad. I'd agree that creased cloth when suspended such that the creases were "settling" would probably show motion. Creased cloth where the creases are running perpendicular to gravity most likely would not move due to gravity as long as the suspension is reasonably stable. Granted, this does depend on the cloth and very fine cloth is more likely to move during an exposure but that's most likely going to be from air currents than anything else.

Also, if your laser is close enough to be causing thermal effects across your table, what the ^$%# is it doing that close? Are you mad?? Put some baffling between the laser and the table if you can't move it farther away but either way, you've got a broken table that needs fixing.

I submit that the problems people have with cloth have less to do with the cloth than it does with their shooting environment.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** Some materials do seem to move "on their own". This is why so many have tried making a hologram of a rose and going through all sorts of gyrations to stop it moving

Roses don't "seem to move", roses *do move*.

They're alive and light sensitive. When put in darkness, the petals do relax. Combine that with the fact that they don't really like to be cut from the parent plant and can't get the nutrients they need and you end up with even more motion.

One way to work around this problem is to keep them as cold as possible and use hot developer, as used by Lon Moore.

posts.content_md:
> **dave battin:** many times i use black felt behind my object ,as the farbric is always moving and makes it appear as if its floating in black space (the object that is,not the fabric)

How long is your settling time? How is the felt suspended? Do you have any vents in your lab (blowing air in)? Are you in the lab at the same time?

Part of the reason I'm chasing this topic is the typically cut-and-dried response that one can't do fabric without it moving. I believe that for most cases (except perhaps for very fine fabric, and I now have on my list to try those) fabric movement can be traced to an unstable shooting environment.

I also use black felt (and velvet) in my backgrounds and I consistently have the opposite problem that if I have any specular reflection hitting the plate, it's quite visible. For the rest, I don't expect to see black fabric anyway.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I've had pretty good luck making holograms of black velveteen ... unfortunately! I'm usually trying to *prevent* recording of the background, or supports for the object. I find that I have to take special steps to *make* the fabric move during the exposure to make it disappear. It may be because I secure everything well to prevent the fabric from drifting into a beam somewhere and wasting an exposure that way. 

I've used black crepe paper instead of fabric. If it's allowed to hang, it'll probably move. Also, black velveteen (cotton based) is better than black velvet (rayon based) because it doesn't have a "sheen" to it. Another good source of a black background is retroreflective paint. It will send the light that hits it (object lighting) back toward its source instead of toward the recording plate.

The thermal effects I was referring to were caused by the energy existing within the illuminating beam of the laser itself. I was not referring to the thermal effects caused by the various electric effects from within the laser head. While the energy within the beam is fairly low, it may be significant . I stress that it's not an effect that's by any means universal, just that for certain materials, motion is caused by transfer of heat from laser to material.

[quote:148ccfd8df="MichaelH"]Roses don't "seem to move", roses do move.

They're alive and light sensitive. When put in darkness, the petals do relax. Combine that with the fact that they don't really like to be cut from the parent plant and can't get the nutrients they need and you end up with even more motion.

One way to work around this problem is to keep them as cold as possible and use hot developer, as used by Lon Moore.[/quote:148ccfd8df]

I'm afraid I'm not sure of the distinction between "seems to" and "does" in a colloquial sense. Certainly, something that "seems to do" something can be concieved as actaully doing it, hence it may seem to do it because it does do it. I might suggest that the distinction is based more on colloquial tautology, which is common in high level languages, than a distinction of purpose. Of course, if something "seems to do" something and doesn't then we're subject to an illusion. My statement was not meant to imply an illusionar y effect, but a real one. The cause might, however, be illusionary. In any case, this was observed and reported by Rob Mundy (formerly Richmond Holographics and now Spatial Imaging [http://www.holograms.co.uk/background.html](http://www.holograms.co.uk/background.html) ). I'm afraid he has far more experience than I concerning the process of holography and he was relating his experiences with shooting roses. It might well be that he was ignorant or inept in his holography. Please take it up with him. I believe his email is on the site.

[quote:148ccfd8df="MichaelH"]Part of the reason I'm chasing this topic is the typically cut-and-dried response that one can't do fabric without it moving. I believe that for most cases (except perhaps for very fine fabric, and I now have on my list to try those) fabric movement can be traced to an unstable shooting environment. [/quote:148ccfd8df]

All movement, indeed all variations, in the process of holography can always be traced to some cause. I have to believe as a scientist that nothing in holography is supernatural. In my experience, the root problem lies not in discovering the cause, but in ascertaining wehther or not it's cost-effective in terms of time and effort to simply by-pass it. To some holography is a precise and completely controllable technical feat and the more control is used, the more exact the results, while to others, the holographic image is merely aesthetic and if the aesthetic ism can be created with a minimum effort so much the better. I've known Peter Miller throw off a piece in a matter of hours while I collaborated with him on a piece that took days.
